questions.question: Which statement gives the working description of $\mathbb R$ used in Math I: Calculus?
options: The complete ordered number system represented by the real line
The finite ordered list of all positive rational numbers
The number system obtained by allowing a zero denominator
The unordered collection of all subsets of rational numbers
questions.explanation: The course treats $\mathbb R$ as the complete ordered number system represented by the real number line. Completeness means that the rational line's gaps are filled and appears through least upper bounds and convergence results.
questions.tested_skill: recognise the course description of real numbers
questions.source_support: The real numbers form the complete ordered number system represented by the real number line.
questions.polish_notes: Removed student-facing page/excerpt wording; Polished wording without changing option order or correct answer
option_explanations: The positive rationals are neither finite nor all of $\mathbb R$; negative and irrational reals are missing.
Allowing a zero denominator creates undefined expressions rather than real numbers.
A collection of subsets is not the ordered number system on which real arithmetic is performed.
questions.rewrite_notes: Replaced the retired Cauchy-sequence construction with the course's working description of the reals.

questions.question: Which notation denotes the set of all real numbers?
options: $\mathbb{Q}$
$\mathbb{R}$
$\mathbb{Z}$
$\mathbb{N}$
questions.explanation: The standard notation for the set containing all rational and irrational real numbers is $\mathbb R$.
questions.source_support: The set of all real numbers is denoted by $\mathbb{R}$.
questions.polish_notes: Removed internal key-result/example/page wording and strengthened visible distractors where targeted; Quality round 9: rebalanced correct-answer positions to remove option-index guessing cue
option_explanations: $\mathbb Q$ contains only rational reals.
$\mathbb Z$ contains only integers.
$\mathbb N$ contains only natural numbers.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).

questions.question: Which of the following numbers is real but not rational?
options: $\sqrt{2}$
The set $\mathbb{Q}$
questions.explanation: The number $\sqrt2$ is a real number, but no ratio of integers has square equal to $2$. It is therefore irrational.
questions.source_support: The number $\sqrt2$ is real but not rational.
questions.polish_notes: Removed internal key-result/example/page wording and strengthened visible distractors where targeted; Quality round 9: rebalanced correct-answer positions to remove option-index guessing cue
option_explanations: The value $1/2$ is explicitly a ratio of integers, so it is rational as well as real.
The expression $0/0$ is undefined and does not denote a real number.
The symbol $\mathbb Q$ denotes a set of numbers, not an individual real number.
questions.rewrite_notes: Removed construction-based justification and retired quotient notation.

questions.question: Which statement correctly classifies the integer $-3$ using the number-system inclusions?
options: It belongs to $\mathbb Z$ but not to $\mathbb Q$.
It belongs to $\mathbb Z$, $\mathbb Q$, and $\mathbb R$.
It belongs to $\mathbb Q$ but not to $\mathbb Z$.
It belongs to $\mathbb R$ but not to $\mathbb Q$.
questions.explanation: Every integer is rational because $a=a/1$, and every rational is real. Hence $-3$ belongs to $\mathbb Z$, $\mathbb Q$, and $\mathbb R$.
questions.source_support: The course uses $\mathbb N\subset\mathbb Z\subset\mathbb Q\subset\mathbb R$.
questions.polish_notes: Quality round 9: rebalanced correct-answer positions to remove option-index guessing cue
option_explanations: Every integer is rational, so $-3=-3/1$ also belongs to $\mathbb Q$.
The number $-3$ is a signed whole number, so excluding it from $\mathbb Z$ is incorrect.
Since $-3=-3/1$, it is rational and cannot lie in $\mathbb R\setminus\mathbb Q$.
questions.rewrite_notes: Replaced the retired sequence-construction question with number-system inclusion.

questions.question: Which property of $\mathbb R$ expresses the completeness used in this course?
options: Every sequence of real numbers converges to a real limit
Every nonempty real set bounded above has a least upper bound
Every real number can be expressed as a ratio of integers
Every pair of integers has an integer quotient
questions.explanation: The least-upper-bound property says that each nonempty subset of $\mathbb R$ bounded above has a supremum in $\mathbb R$. This is the form of completeness used to distinguish $\mathbb R$ from $\mathbb Q$.
questions.source_support: Every nonempty subset of $\mathbb R$ bounded above has a least upper bound.
questions.polish_notes: Quality round 9: rebalanced correct-answer positions to remove option-index guessing cue
option_explanations: Some real sequences diverge, such as $1,2,3,\ldots$, so completeness does not make every sequence converge.
Irrational numbers such as $\sqrt2$ cannot be expressed as ratios of integers.
The quotient $1/2$ is not an integer, so integers are not closed under division.
questions.rewrite_notes: Replaced equality of Cauchy representatives with the course's least-upper-bound form of completeness.

questions.question: What role do real numbers play relative to rational numbers?
options: They remove all irrational numbers from arithmetic.
They make limits impossible to define.
They replace sequences by unordered sets.
They complete the rational numbers by filling limiting gaps.
questions.explanation: The real completion adds limits missing from $\mathbb Q$, such as the value approached by rational approximations to $\sqrt2$.
questions.tested_skill: explain the extension from rationals to reals
questions.source_support: Real numbers complete the rationals by filling limiting gaps.
questions.polish_notes: Quality round 9: rebalanced correct-answer positions to remove option-index guessing cue
option_explanations: Irrationals are added to, not removed from, the rational number line.
The real system makes limits exact numerical objects rather than impossible to define.
Real numbers extend the rational number system; they do not replace sequences by sets.
questions.rewrite_notes: Removed residual construction language from the distractor explanations.

questions.question: Let $E\subseteq\mathbb R$ be nonempty and bounded above. What does completeness guarantee?
options: The set $E$ has a largest element in $E$.
The set $E$ has a smallest element in $E$.
Every upper bound of $E$ is a rational in $E$.
The set $E$ has a unique least upper bound in $\mathbb R$.
questions.explanation: Completeness guarantees a supremum: a least upper bound in $\mathbb R$. The supremum need not belong to $E$, so it need not be a maximum.
questions.source_support: A nonempty subset of $\mathbb R$ bounded above has exactly one least upper bound.
questions.polish_notes: Removed internal key-result/example/page wording and strengthened visible distractors where targeted; Quality round 9: rebalanced correct-answer positions to remove option-index guessing cue
option_explanations: A bounded set need not contain its supremum; for example, $(0,1)$ has no largest element.
Being bounded above gives no guarantee of a smallest element or even of being bounded below.
An upper bound need not be rational or belong to the set it bounds.
questions.rewrite_notes: Replaced a formal limit-object question with an application of completeness.

questions.question: How are the real numbers split by rationality?
options: A real number can be neither rational nor irrational.
Every irrational number is excluded from $\mathbb{R}$.
Every real number is either rational or irrational.
Only rational numbers can be limits of rational sequences.
questions.explanation: Because $\mathbb Q\subseteq\mathbb R$, each real either belongs to $\mathbb Q$ or to its complement $\mathbb R\setminus\mathbb Q$.
questions.skill_detail: every real is rational or irrational
questions.source_support: Every real number is either rational or irrational.
questions.rewrite_notes: Replaced residual construction language with the course's rational-approximation example.
option_explanations: The rational and irrational cases exhaust $\mathbb R$, so there is no third type of real number.
Irrational numbers are precisely the real numbers outside $\mathbb Q$, so they remain inside $\mathbb R$.
Rational approximations such as $1.4,1.41,1.414,\ldots$ can approach the irrational real $\sqrt2$.

questions.question: Which statement describes the density of $\mathbb Q$ in $\mathbb R$?
options: Every bounded real set has a least upper bound.
Between any two distinct real numbers lies a rational number.
Every real number can be written as a ratio of integers.
Every sequence of rational numbers is eventually constant.
questions.explanation: Density means that if $x<y$ are real, then some rational $q$ satisfies $x<q<y$. Repeating the argument yields infinitely many rationals between the two reals.
questions.source_support: Between any two distinct real numbers lies a rational number.
questions.polish_notes: Quality round 9: rebalanced correct-answer positions to remove option-index guessing cue
option_explanations: This is the least-upper-bound property of $\mathbb R$, not density of the rationals.
Irrational reals such as $\sqrt2$ cannot be expressed as ratios of integers.
The rational sequence $1,1/2,1/3,\ldots$ is not eventually constant, so this statement is false.
questions.rewrite_notes: Replaced Cauchy-equivalence content with the current density result.

questions.question: Which statement best captures the phrase “filling in all limiting gaps”?
options: Rational numbers stop being numbers inside $\mathbb{R}$.
Every sequence of rational numbers is automatically finite.
Limits of rational sequences become exact numerical objects.
Irrational numbers are removed from the number system.
questions.explanation: The rationals omit exact values such as $\sqrt2$, even though rational approximations can approach them arbitrarily closely. The real number system contains these missing values, so limits can be exact numbers in $\mathbb R$.
questions.source_support: Real numbers fill the gaps left by the rationals and allow limits to be exact numerical objects.
questions.polish_notes: Quality round 9: rebalanced correct-answer positions to remove option-index guessing cue
option_explanations: Rational numbers remain a subset of $\mathbb R$ after the gaps are filled.
A rational sequence may be infinite; finiteness is unrelated to whether its limiting value is real.
Irrational values such as $\sqrt2$ are included in $\mathbb R$, not removed from it.
questions.rewrite_notes: Removed Cauchy-construction language while retaining the supported completeness interpretation.

questions.question: For $x=10$ and $\varepsilon=0.03$, which positive integer $M$ verifies the Archimedean inequality $M\varepsilon>x$?
questions.explanation: We need $0.03M>10$, or $M>333\frac13$. The integer $M=334$ works because $334(0.03)=10.02>10$.
questions.source_support: For positive reals $x,\varepsilon$, some positive integer $M$ satisfies $M\varepsilon>x$.
questions.polish_notes: Quality round 9: rebalanced correct-answer positions to remove option-index guessing cue
option_explanations: The product $33(0.03)=0.99$ is far below $10$.
The product $333(0.03)=9.99$ is still slightly below $10$.
The product $300(0.03)=9$ does not exceed $10$.
questions.rewrite_notes: Replaced equivalence of Cauchy representatives with a current-course Archimedean application.

questions.question: What can safely be concluded about $\sqrt2$?
options: It is rational because decimal approximations exist.
It is a real number and it is irrational.
It is undefined because no rational squares to $2$.
It is an integer strictly between $1$ and $2$.
questions.explanation: The real number system contains the positive number whose square is $2$, while the parity argument shows that no rational has this property. Therefore $\sqrt2\in\mathbb R\setminus\mathbb Q$.
questions.source_support: The number $\sqrt2$ is real but not rational.
questions.polish_notes: Reworded MCQ stem to ask the mathematical question directly rather than referring to a choice/option.; Removed internal key-result/example/page wording and strengthened visible distractors where targeted; Quality round 9: rebalanced correct-answer positions to remove option-index guessing cue
option_explanations: Having rational approximations does not make a number rational; $\sqrt2$ is the relevant counterexample.
Failure to find a rational square root shows irrationality, not that the real square root is undefined.
There is no integer strictly between $1$ and $2$, and $\sqrt2$ is not an integer.
questions.rewrite_notes: Removed the Cauchy-sequence construction from the justification.

questions.question: What is the relationship between $\mathbb{Q}$ and $\mathbb{R}$?
options: $\mathbb{Q}\subseteq\mathbb{R}$
$\mathbb{R}\subseteq\mathbb{Q}$
they are disjoint
$\mathbb{Q}=\mathbb{R}$
questions.explanation: Every integer ratio is a real number, so the rational set is contained in the real set: $\mathbb Q\subseteq\mathbb R$.
questions.source_support: The number-system chain includes $\mathbb Q\subseteq\mathbb R$.
questions.rewrite_notes: Updated source support to the course's direct number-system viewpoint.
option_explanations: Irrationals such as $\sqrt2$ lie in $\mathbb R$ but not $\mathbb Q$, disproving the reverse inclusion.
The sets overlap in every rational number and are not disjoint.
They are not equal because $\mathbb R$ also contains irrationals.

questions.question: Between any two distinct real numbers, how many rational numbers lie?
options: Infinitely many
Exactly one
None
Exactly two
questions.explanation: Density gives one rational between any two reals, and repeatedly applying it to smaller subintervals gives infinitely many.
questions.source_support: The density of $\mathbb Q$ in $\mathbb R$ places a rational between any two distinct reals.
questions.rewrite_notes: Updated source support to the explicit density result on the current concept page.
option_explanations: After finding one rational, each side still contains another, so uniqueness fails.
Density of $\mathbb Q$ in $\mathbb R$ rules out an empty interval between distinct reals.
The iterative argument produces more than two rationals.

questions.question: If $x<y$ and $z>0$ are real numbers, which relation must hold?
options: $xz>yz$
$xz=yz$
$xz<yz$
$x+z>y+z$
questions.explanation: Multiplying both sides of a strict inequality by a positive real number preserves its direction. Therefore $x<y$ and $z>0$ imply $xz<yz$.
questions.source_support: If $x<y$ and $z>0$, then $xz<yz$.
questions.rewrite_notes: Replaced out-of-scope cardinality content with a current real-order property.
option_explanations: The inequality reverses only when multiplying by a negative number, not by positive $z$.
Because $z>0$, equality $xz=yz$ would force $x=y$, contradicting $x<y$.
Adding the same number preserves order, so the correct additive relation would be $x+z<y+z$.

questions.question: Which conclusion connects completeness of $\mathbb R$ to the monotone convergence theorem?
options: Every bounded increasing real sequence converges to its supremum.
Every sequence of real numbers converges to a finite value.
Every bounded real sequence must be increasing.
Every rational sequence has a rational limit.
questions.explanation: For an increasing sequence bounded above, completeness supplies the supremum of its terms, and the monotone convergence theorem identifies that supremum as the limit. The other statements impose no conditions sufficient for convergence.
questions.source_support: Completeness enters through suprema and the monotone convergence theorem.
questions.rewrite_notes: Replaced Cauchy-completeness wording with the course's supremum-based convergence result.
option_explanations: A sequence such as $1,-1,1,-1,\ldots$ is real-valued but does not converge.
Boundedness alone does not imply monotonicity; $(-1)^n$ is a counterexample.
Rational terms can converge to an irrational real number, so the limit need not be rational.

questions.question: Which classification is possible for $\sqrt2$?
options: Rational but not real
Neither real nor irrational
Natural and equal to $2$
Real and irrational
questions.explanation: The number $\sqrt2$ belongs to $\mathbb R$ but not $\mathbb Q$, so its classification is real and irrational.
questions.source_support: $\sqrt2$ is real but not rational.
questions.polish_notes: Quality round 9: rebalanced correct-answer positions to remove option-index guessing cue
questions.skill_detail: Classify a standard real number example.
option_explanations: Every rational is real, and $\sqrt2$ is not rational.
It satisfies both real and irrational membership.
$\sqrt2\ne2$ because squaring would give $2\ne4$.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).

questions.question: Which set contains $\pi$?
options: $\mathbb Q\setminus\mathbb Z$
$\mathbb Z$
$\mathbb N$
$\mathbb R\setminus\mathbb Q$
questions.explanation: The number $\pi$ is real and irrational, so it lies in $\mathbb R$ but not in $\mathbb Q$. Hence $\pi\in\mathbb R\setminus\mathbb Q$.
questions.source_support: The number $\pi$ is real but not rational.
questions.polish_notes: Quality round 9: rebalanced correct-answer positions to remove option-index guessing cue
questions.skill_detail: Connect convergent rational sequences to real numbers.
option_explanations: This set contains non-integer rationals, but $\pi$ is not rational.
Integers are signed whole numbers, whereas $\pi$ is not a whole number.
Natural numbers are nonnegative whole numbers, and $\pi$ is not one of them.
questions.rewrite_notes: Replaced a sequence-as-construction question with direct classification in the current number systems.

questions.question: What does it mean that real numbers complete the rational numbers?
options: They remove all rational numbers
They make every sequence divergent.
They consist only of integers
They fill limiting gaps left by rationals.
questions.explanation: The rationals are dense but still omit exact values such as $\sqrt2$. The real number system fills these gaps, which is reflected in its completeness and least-upper-bound property.
questions.source_support: Real numbers fill the gaps left by rational numbers.
questions.polish_notes: Quality round 9: rebalanced correct-answer positions to remove option-index guessing cue
option_explanations: Rational numbers remain a subset of the real system after completion.
Completeness supplies missing limit and least-upper-bound values rather than forcing divergence.
Integers form only a proper subset of the real number system.
questions.rewrite_notes: Removed Cauchy-sequence construction language from the explanation.

questions.question: Which statement follows for every $x\in\mathbb R$?
options: $x$ is both rational and irrational
$x$ is always a natural number
$x$ is either an integer or not real
$x$ is rational or irrational
questions.explanation: The rational subset $\mathbb Q$ and its complement $\mathbb R\setminus\mathbb Q$ partition $\mathbb R$. Thus every real is exactly one of rational or irrational.
questions.source_support: Every real number is either rational or irrational.
questions.polish_notes: Removed internal key-result/example/page wording and strengthened visible distractors where targeted; Quality round 9: rebalanced correct-answer positions to remove option-index guessing cue
option_explanations: The rational and irrational subsets are disjoint, so no real number belongs to both.
Numbers such as $-1/2$ and $\sqrt2$ are real but not natural.
A non-integer such as $1/2$ is still real, so this proposed alternative is false.
questions.rewrite_notes: Removed the obsolete limit-object distractor and aligned the choices with current classifications.
